blindSummary:
This country carries serious danger for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation (an international human-rights organisation, 2024) shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition (a medicalised registration route exists on paper under the civil-status law), no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids + registry practices + zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
blindOutOfScope: Registry practices and raid patterns target residents but define the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.
blindSourceSummaries: International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2024) on the systematic denial of human rights to LGBTIQ people here: documents widespread homophobia/transphobia, the 2016 police register of LGBTIQ people, 2022/2023 police raids with forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges, ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police, privacy violations followed by 'pornography' prosecutions, and additional problems facing trans people.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex acts not criminalised since independence; no SOGIESC non-discrimination protections; no transparent legal gender recognition procedure, though at least two trans men and one trans woman changed markers via court in 2023; nonconsensual intersex interventions legal; in 2024 a regional LGBT network recorded 27 cases of human-rights violations against LGBT people, with arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion by police.

Study by a regional LGBT network (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across this country's wider region (with in-country coordinators), including information for trans migrants.

Regional LGBTI organisation's annual review 2025, country chapter (covering 2024): anti-LGBTI laws in a foreign state have influenced the local approach; coming out risks family shame leading to sham marriages - one person was beaten, tied up without food and forcibly married, with police taking no action; in one region, 10+ cases of police luring LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database and extort money; the 2022 anti-discrimination law dropped SOGI, leaving only 'sex'.

Legislative analysis by a regional LGBT network and local partners (2020) on law related to SOGI and HIV here: identifies legal barriers for gay men, other MSM and trans people, analysing legislation and law-enforcement practice against international standards.

International human-rights organisation's world report (2017), chapter on this country: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 - opposition leaders sentenced, lawyers imprisoned, a predetermined referendum allowing the president to rule for life - the repressive context for LGBT life.

Citizen-media outlet (Jan 2013): an article reporting that this country remains hostile territory for gay people - despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier, there is very little tolerance; those who come out become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police; the LGBT community remains one of the most closed and secretive parts of society; sparked by a violent university incident.
blindLocalsOnly: The informal LGBT registries and the on-paper medicalised legal-gender-recognition route are resident-facing; the raid pattern primarily targets residents but defines the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.
